ALPHABET = '123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz'
def b58(data):
    n = int.from_bytes(data, 'big')

    while n:

    zeros = len(data) - len(data.lstrip(b'\x00'))

title: The Blockchain

nodes.label: Block structure
nodes.body: The first section of the chapter opens the block: a header of six fields and a list of transactions, with the sizes, the version flags, the time and the target that the header carries (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Each statement was checked against a real block, the genesis block, block 277,315 or block 840,000, or against a block of the test chain (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Block container; Header fields.

nodes.label: Block container
nodes.body: This subject asks what a block is as a container: the header, the counter and the transactions, the size field that belongs to the file on disk, the weight limit and the fields that getblock prints today (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers Block is header plus transactions; The block size field is file storage; Transaction counter; The getblock output today; Block reserved weight.

nodes.label: Block is header plus transactions
nodes.body: A block is a container: a small header of metadata, then a counter that says how many transactions follow, then the transactions themselves, which make up nearly all of the bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The genesis block shows the arithmetic exactly: 80 bytes of header, 1 byte for the counter and 204 bytes for its single coinbase transaction make 285 bytes, the size that mempool.space lists for block 0 (Mempool Space, 2026). On the private test chain run for this chapter, blocks holding 1, 2, 3 and 4 transactions measured 250, 472, 694 and 915 bytes, so each added transaction cost about 222 bytes, which is why a block grows almost in a straight line with its transaction count (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Think of a parcel: a shipping label of fixed size on the outside, a packing list that says how many items are inside, and then the items, which decide how heavy the parcel is.

nodes.definition: A block is the 80-byte header, then a counter of the transactions, then the transactions themselves: the genesis block is 80 + 1 + 204 = 285 bytes, and the blocks of the private test chain with 1, 2, 3 and 4 transactions are 250, 472, 694 and 915 bytes, about 222 bytes more for each added transaction.

nodes.label: The block size field is file storage
nodes.body: The first table of the chapter starts with a 4-byte field called block size, but that field belongs to the way Bitcoin Core stores blocks on disk and not to the block as it travels between nodes or as consensus sees it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the blk files each block is written as 4 magic bytes, then 4 bytes giving the size of the block, then the block, and since release 28.0 the whole file is scrambled with a random key kept in a file named xor.dat (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024). Reading the first bytes of the test chain's blk00000.dat gave nonsense until the key d462ed9f917fe79d was applied; then the file began fabfb5da, the magic of the test chain, followed by 1d010000, which is the little-endian number 285, the size of the genesis block, and the genesis block that followed equalled the one the node reported (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The chain data at height 0 occupied 293 bytes on disk, which is 285 plus the 8 bytes of magic and size. The release notes warn that older releases and external software cannot read such a directory, and the scrambling is like a diary in a private code: the owner reads it with the key, a stranger who opens the file sees noise.

nodes.label: Transaction counter
nodes.body: After the header comes a counter of transactions written as a compactSize integer, a number format that takes 1 byte for values up to 252, 3 bytes for 253 to 65,535 and 5 bytes beyond that (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). The book says the counter takes 1 to 3 bytes, which is right because a block cannot hold more than 65,535 transactions: the smallest possible transaction weighs 4 x 60 = 240 weight units, so the limit of 4,000,000 allows at most 16,666 of them (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Real blocks are far from that bound, block 840,000 had 3,050 transactions and so spent 3 bytes on its counter. A compactSize number is like the page-number system of a book: small numbers get a short mark, and only a very thick book needs the long form.
nodes.definition: The transaction counter is a compactSize integer of 1 byte up to 252, 3 bytes for 253 to 65,535 and 5 bytes from 65,536, and a block cannot hold more than 4,000,000 / 240 = 16,666 transactions because the smallest transaction weighs 240 weight units, so the book's 1 to 3 bytes are enough.

nodes.label: The getblock output today
nodes.body: The book prints the answer of getblock for the genesis block, and anyone who runs the command today sees a listing that is longer. Bitcoin Core 29.0 added the field target, the 256-bit number the block hash had to stay under, and 31.0 added an object coinbase_tx that carries the version, locktime, sequence, coinbase script and witness of the first transaction, so a program can read the coinbase without fetching the full transaction list (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). On the test chain the genesis block listing contained exactly these two fields beyond the book's, and lacked only nextblockhash, because no second block existed yet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). None of this changes what a block is; it is the same record with two more labelled drawers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a bank statement that gains two new lines after a software update: the old numbers are all still there and still add up.

nodes.label: Block reserved weight
nodes.body: A miner's block template does not fill the consensus limit to the last unit, because room must be kept for the header, the transaction counter and the coinbase that the mining software adds later. Bitcoin Core reserves 8,000 weight units by default with the option -blockreservedweight, so the fullest template it builds is 4,000,000 - 8,000 = 3,992,000 weight units, a number that release 29.0 names when it explains a bug that had reserved the 4,000 units twice (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). Block 840,000 weighed 3,993,281 weight units, more than that, so it was built by other software with a smaller reserve (Mempool Space, 2026). The book speaks only of the limit of about 4,000,000 bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a lift that is rated for 1,000 kg but whose operator leaves room for the attendant: the rating is the law, the sign on the door is the habit. This example reads mempool_block_840000.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. nodes.label: Header fields
nodes.body: This subject asks what is in the 80 bytes: the version bits, the field order and byte order, the timestamp and the median of eleven, the compact target and the nonce that is too small for the work (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). This subject covers The header is 80 bytes; Block weight limit; Version bits field; Field order and endianness; Timestamp field; Median time past; Target compact encoding; Nonce and extra nonce.

nodes.label: The header is 80 bytes
nodes.body: Every Bitcoin block header is exactly 80 bytes: 4 for the version, 32 for the previous block hash, 32 for the merkle root, 4 each for the time, the target and the nonce (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The genesis header, the header of block 277,315 and a header of the test chain all parse to 80 bytes in the code of this chapter, and because a serialized block may be at most 4,000,000 bytes, a full block is 4,000,000 / 80 = 50,000 times the size of its header, the figure the book gives as almost 50,000 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The fixed size is what makes light clients possible: a phone can keep all 971,538 headers of today's chain in about 78 megabytes, since 971,538 x 80 bytes is 77.7 million bytes, while the whole chain is some 775,000 megabytes (Blockchain Charts, 2026). A header is like the spine label of a book on a library shelf: always the same size, enough to find the book and check that it is the right one, while the pages stay on the shelf. This example reads mempool_header_0.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: ([80, 80, 80], 50000, '4000000', True)
nodes.definition: Every header, of the genesis block, of block 277,315 and of block 120 of the test chain, is exactly 80 bytes, and since MAX_BLOCK_SERIALIZED_SIZE is 4,000,000 a full block can be 4,000,000 / 80 = 50,000 times the header, the book's 'almost 50,000 times'.

nodes.label: Block weight limit
nodes.body: The book says that the transactions of a block can total about 4,000,000 bytes, but the rule that consensus enforces is a limit of 4,000,000 weight units, in which every byte of a transaction counts four times except the witness data, which counts once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The test chain shows the formula: its block 120 had a size of 249 bytes, a stripped size of 213 bytes (without witness data) and a weight of 888, which is 3 x 213 + 249. Block 840,000 on the main chain held 3,050 transactions with a weight of 3,993,281, which is 99.83 percent of the limit, while its size was only 2,325,617 bytes, about 762 bytes per transaction, so a block full by weight is smaller than 4,000,000 bytes (Mempool Space, 2026). It is like a lorry with a weight limit and not a size limit: a load of feathers and a load of bricks fill the same lorry in very different volumes. nodes.label: Version bits field
nodes.body: The version field started as a plain version number, 1 for the genesis block and 2 for block 277,315, but it is now a row of 32 flags (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP 9 lets miners signal readiness for a soft fork by setting one bit each, and requires the top three bits to be 001 so that the number stays at least 0x20000000, which is what every block of the test chain carries (Wuille et al., 2015). The draft BIP 320 goes further and reserves sixteen bits, from bit 13 to bit 28 (the mask 0x1fffe000), for miners to use as extra nonce space; block 840,000 carries 0x2a5fe000, which has bits inside that mask set, and the BIP is still a Draft with a proposed replacement, BIP 323 (BtcDrak, 2018); (Mempool Space, 2026). The version field is like the dashboard of a car: it began as one dial and now has a row of small warning lamps, some for the manufacturer and some left free for the driver. nodes.label: Field order and endianness
nodes.body: The six fields of the header sit in a fixed order in the 80 bytes: version, previous block hash, merkle root, time, bits, nonce (Bitcoin Project, 2026). Integers are stored least significant byte first, so the version 2 appears as 02000000, and the two hashes are stored in the reverse of the order in which people display them, which is why a hash that begins with many zeros when printed ends with them in the raw header. Rebuilding block 277,315 from its decoded fields in exactly this order gave back the 80 bytes that mempool.space returns, with the bits 1903a30c at the end of the target bytes and the parent hash ending a1632249 in display order (Mempool Space, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Little-endian is like writing a date as day, month, year when you are used to the opposite: nothing is wrong, but you must know which convention a file uses before you read it. nodes.label: Timestamp field
nodes.body: The timestamp is a 4-byte count of seconds since 1 January 1970, the Unix time, and the book calls it the approximate creation time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The genesis block says 1231006505, which is 2009-01-03 18:15:05 UTC, block 840,000 says 2024-04-20 00:09:27 UTC, and a node refuses a block whose time is more than 2 x 60 x 60 = 7,200 seconds ahead of its own clock (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Because the counter is 4 bytes, it can only run until 2106-02-07 06:28:15 UTC, the overflow date that Unix time discussions mention and that Optech lists among the consequences of the timewarp fix of BIP 54 (Wikipedia contributors, 2026); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). A block's timestamp is like the date stamp on a letter: roughly right is good enough, but the post office will not accept one dated far in the future. nodes.label: Median time past
nodes.body: A block's timestamp must be greater than the median of the timestamps of the previous 11 blocks, and BIP 113 uses this median time past as the clock for time locks, because it cannot be moved far by a single miner (Kerin and Friedenbach, 2015). Bitcoin Core keeps nMedianTimeSpan = 11 and computes it in GetMedianTimePast (Bitcoin Core, 2026). On the test chain the median of blocks 111 to 121 was 1792052132, equal to the value that the node itself reported for block 121, and on the real chain block 277,315 has a timestamp 1,651 seconds later than its median time past, which shows that the median can run behind the wall clock by about 27 minutes (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). It is like judging the time by the middle value of eleven clocks in a room: one clock that runs wrong cannot change the middle. nodes.label: Target compact encoding
nodes.body: The target is the number the block hash must not exceed, and the header stores it in 4 bytes as a floating-point style 'compact' form: one byte of exponent and three of mantissa, so that target = mantissa x 256^(exponent - 3) (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). The value 0x1d00ffff, that of the genesis block and the lowest difficulty ever used on mainnet, expands to 0xffff followed by 26 zero bytes and equals a difficulty of 1; the 0x1903a30c of block 277,315 gives a difficulty of 1,180,923,195.258, the number in the book's listing; and the test chain's 0x207fffff expands to the target 7fffff followed by zeros, which the node itself printed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The work of one block at difficulty 1 is 0x100010001, the chain work printed for the genesis block. The compact form is like scientific notation on a pocket calculator: it keeps the first few digits and the size of the number, and throws away the digits nobody needs. This example reads mempool_block_277315.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: ('0xffff0000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000', 1180923195.2580261, True, 1180923195.2580261, '0x100010001', True)
nodes.definition: The 4-byte target field packs a 256-bit number as one byte of exponent and three of mantissa: 0x1d00ffff is the target 0xffff followed by 26 zero bytes (difficulty 1, the genesis block and chain work 0x100010001), the field 0x1903a30c of block 277,315 gives a difficulty of 1,180,923,195.258, which is the value in the book's listing, and 0x207fffff on the test chain gives the target 7fffff followed by zeros.

nodes.label: Nonce and extra nonce
nodes.body: The nonce is the 4-byte number that miners change again and again to get a different hash, and it is here that the proof of work happens, as the next chapter of the book explains (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). But 4 bytes give only 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 tries, and at the difficulty of block 277,315 a block took about 5 x 10^18 hashes, 1,180,941,215 times as many, so a miner must change something else when the nonce runs out: the extra nonce in the coinbase script, spare bits of the version field, or the timestamp, as the mining chapter says (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Block 277,315 itself was found with nonce 4215469401, near the upper end, while the blocks of the private test chain, at the lowest difficulty, needed only nonce 1 (Mempool Space, 2026). It is like a combination lock with only four digits: when the digits are used up you must reset something else in the lock to go on trying. This example reads mempool_block_277315.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: (4294967296, 4215469401, 1180941215, 1, True)

nodes.label: Block identifiers
nodes.body: The second section teaches the two names of a block, the hash that is computed from the header and the height that counts the blocks, and why the first is unique and the second is not (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also covers the coinbase rules that depend on height: the height written in the coinbase and the 100 blocks of maturity (Andresen, 2012). This subject covers Hash identity; Height and maturity.

nodes.label: Hash identity
nodes.body: This subject asks what the block hash is: a double SHA-256 of the header, which is not stored inside the block and whose zeros are a consequence of the target (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). This subject covers Block hash is double sha256; Hash not stored in block; Hash leading zeros.

nodes.label: Block hash is double sha256
nodes.body: The block hash is the SHA-256 of the SHA-256 of the 80-byte header, and nothing else is hashed: the transactions are covered only through the merkle root inside the header (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). Hashing the genesis header twice gives 000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172b3f1b60a8ce26f once the bytes are reversed for display, a single SHA-256 gives something unrelated beginning 6dd6c5716cc8e243, and the header of block 277,315 hashes to the id that mempool.space lists (Mempool Space, 2026). In the source the hash is the one line return (HashWriter{} << *this).GetHash(); of CBlockHeader::GetHash (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A cryptographic hash is a fingerprint: change one bit of the finger and the print changes completely, which is why the header can stand for the whole block (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). It is like the seal on a bottle of medicine, small but impossible to copy onto a changed bottle. This example reads mempool_header_0.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. nodes.definition: The block hash is the SHA-256 of the SHA-256 of the 80-byte header: the genesis header gives 000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172b3f1b60a8ce26f (displayed byte-reversed), whereas a single SHA-256 gives 6dd6c5716cc8e243 and so on, and the header of block 277,315 hashes to the id that mempool.space lists.

nodes.label: Hash not stored in block
nodes.body: The block hash is not a field of the block: each node computes it when the block arrives, and may then keep it in an index for fast lookup (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The 285 bytes of the test chain's genesis block contain neither its hash 0f9188f1... nor the reverse of that hash, but the header of the next block does contain the reversed hash as its previous-block field, so the name of a block is written down by its child and not by itself (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The reason is simple logic: a block cannot contain a hash of itself, because the hash would have to be known before the content that it is the hash of. It is like a person who cannot sign a letter with a name that has not yet been given: it is the next page of the register that records the name.

nodes.label: Hash leading zeros
nodes.body: Block hashes famously begin with many zeros, but the zeros are not stored or demanded as such: they are the visible result of the rule that the hash, read as a number, must not exceed the target (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). The genesis hash begins with 10 zero hexadecimal digits, block 277,315 with 15 and block 840,000 with 19, and each of the first two was checked in the code to be no larger than the target in its own header (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). On the test chain, whose target 7fff... is the easiest possible, the genesis hash 0f9188f1... has a single zero. More zeros mean a smaller target and therefore more work, as when a lottery draws only the numbers below a limit and the limit is lowered: the tickets with the winning numbers become rarer. The book does not discuss the zeros here but in the mining chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). nodes.label: Height and maturity
nodes.body: This subject asks what the height is: a count from the genesis block that can be shared by competing blocks, that BIP 34 writes into the coinbase and that decides when a reward may be spent (Andresen, 2012). This subject covers Height is not unique; Height from genesis; BIP 34 height in the coinbase; Coinbase maturity of 100 blocks.

nodes.label: Height is not unique
nodes.body: A block has two names: its hash, which identifies it uniquely, and its height, the count of blocks between it and the genesis block, which does not (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book says in a tip box that a height can be shared by competing blocks, and the test chain showed it: two different children of the same parent were both at height 511, with different hashes and the same previous-block field (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This is why software that needs certainty uses the hash, and treats the height as a position that can change owner when the chain reorganizes. A hash is like a passport number and a height like a seat number: two people may have held the same seat on different days, but nobody else has your passport number.
nodes.definition: A hash names one block, a height does not: on the test chain two children of the same parent were both at height 511 with different hashes, and the book's tip says so in a box.

nodes.label: Height from genesis
nodes.body: The height of a block is its distance from the genesis block, which sits at height 0, so a chain with the tip at height h has h + 1 blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On 2026-10-15 the tip of the main chain was at height 971,537, which means 971,538 blocks and, at one block in ten minutes, about 18.5 years of history, whereas the book says that height 800,000 was reached in mid 2023 (Mempool Space, 2026). Block 840,000, the first with the lower reward of 3.125 coins, has the timestamp 2024-04-20 00:09:27 UTC (Mempool Space, 2026). A fresh node with no data reported height 0 and 0 headers, since it knows only the genesis block (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Height is like the kilometre posts along a motorway: they tell you how far you have come, and they are numbered from the same starting point for everybody. nodes.label: BIP 34 height in the coinbase
nodes.body: In the early chain a block's height was not stored in the block; BIP 34 changed this by requiring the height as the first item of the coinbase script, in the 'minimally encoded serialized CScript' form, and its stated purpose is to make every coinbase transaction unique (Andresen, 2012); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The coinbases of the test chain show how the encoding works: height 17 is 011100 (one byte, the number 0x11), 128 is 02800000 (two bytes, 0x0080, because a single 0x80 would read as negative) and 256 is 02000100, while the small heights 1 to 16 are written as the opcodes OP_1 to OP_16, so height 1 starts 5100 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). All eight recorded prefixes decoded back to their heights in the code of this chapter. The older rule BIP 30, assigned to Pieter Wuille on 2012-02-22, goes at the same problem from another side: a block may not contain a transaction whose identifier matches that of an earlier, not-fully-spent transaction, apart from two historic blocks at heights 91842 and 91880 (Wuille, 2012). It is like the number on a cheque: it does not make the cheque valuable, it makes it different from all the others in the book. nodes.label: Coinbase maturity of 100 blocks
nodes.body: The reward and fees that a miner earns in the coinbase transaction cannot be spent at once but only after the block is 100 blocks deep, because a short reorganization would otherwise destroy coins that had already been spent onward (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The constant is COINBASE_MATURITY = 100 in consensus.h; on the test chain a transaction spending a coinbase at depth 99 was rejected with bad-txns-premature-spend-of-coinbase, the same transaction at depth 100 was accepted, and the node's wallet showed the last 100 blocks of the 500 as immature (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The rule applies to every chain, test chains included, so a developer meets it on regtest first. It is like the cooling period of a cheque paid in from abroad: the bank shows the amount at once but lets you draw on it only after the cheque has really cleared.
nodes.definition: The reward of a block can be spent only once the block is 100 blocks deep: with COINBASE_MATURITY = 100 the test chain refused a spend at depth 99 with bad-txns-premature-spend-of-coinbase and allowed it at depth 100.

nodes.label: Genesis block
nodes.body: The third section is about the first block, which is written into the program, carries the headline of The Times of 3 January 2009 and can be rebuilt from a few numbers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The section also shows what is peculiar about it: its reward can never be spent (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). This subject covers Genesis constants; Genesis quirks.

nodes.label: Genesis constants
nodes.body: This subject asks what the genesis block is made of: the constants in chainparams.cpp, the message, the listing in the book and the transaction shared by most chains (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Genesis hash recomputed; Genesis coinbase message; Genesis hardcoded; Genesis listing matches book; Shared genesis transaction.

nodes.label: Genesis hash recomputed
nodes.body: The genesis block is the one block that no node needs to download, because its numbers are written in the program: chainparams.cpp calls CreateGenesisBlock with the time 1231006505, the nonce 2083236893, the bits 0x1d00ffff, version 1 and a reward of 50 coins (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The code of this chapter rebuilt the 204-byte coinbase transaction from those constants, got the transaction id 4a5e1e4b..., put it in an 80-byte header, and hashed it twice to obtain 000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172b3f1b60a8ce26f, the hash that the book prints (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nothing was fetched from the network for this result, so the genesis block is a computation anyone can repeat. It is like the foundation stone of a building that carries its own date and can be checked against the plans: no one has to take the builder's word for it.

nodes.label: Genesis coinbase message
nodes.body: The only input of the genesis block's single transaction has no previous output to spend, as in every coinbase, and its script carries a free text, here the 69 characters The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The script is a push of the number 486604799 (the bits 0x1d00ffff), a push of the number 4, and a push of the 69 bytes of text, which in hexadecimal begins 04ffff001d010445 and then spells the words (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The text proves that the block cannot have been made before that day, because the newspaper could not be quoted earlier, and it also marks the moment of the financial crisis of 2008 and 2009. It is like holding up the day's newspaper in a photograph of a hostage or a lottery winner: the photograph cannot be older than the paper.

nodes.label: Genesis hardcoded
nodes.body: Every node starts with a chain of at least one block, because the genesis block is compiled into the program and cannot be changed, so it is the root from which a trusted chain is built (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A Bitcoin Core 31.1 node started on the private test chain, with no peers and no data directory, reported height 0, 0 headers and 293 bytes of chain data, and the hash it called its best block equalled the genesis hash that the code of this chapter rebuilt from the regtest constants of chainparams.cpp (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A new node can therefore check any chain it is offered by following the parent links back to a block it already knows. It is like a family tree in which the oldest ancestor is printed on the first page: a visitor with a name can follow the line back until it reaches that page, and has no need to ask anybody who is on it.

The chainwork shown in the listing ends in 100010001, which is the number 0x100010001 = 4,295,032,833, the work of one block at difficulty 1, as the code of this chapter computed (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The only things that have aged are the confirmations, 790,496 when the book was written and now over 971,000, and two fields that later releases added. A listing like this is a reference photograph: it has not changed, but the world around it has. nodes.label: Shared genesis transaction
nodes.body: Mainnet, testnet3, signet and regtest all start with the very same coinbase transaction, the 204-byte one with the id 4a5e1e4b... and the message from The Times, and differ only in the header around it: the time, the nonce and the bits (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Testnet4 breaks the pattern: its genesis coinbase is 180 bytes long, has the id 7aa0a7ae... and carries the message 03/May/2024 followed by a 64-digit hexadecimal number in the form of a block hash, in the manner of the headline in the first genesis block (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Jahr, 2024). A shared transaction means shared coinbase text, which is why the regtest genesis block on a laptop also says The Times, and why the book's regtest listing and mainnet listing share the same merkle root 4a5e1e4b... (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a school that prints the same cover on every notebook: the covers are alike and only the pages inside differ.

nodes.label: Genesis quirks
nodes.body: This subject asks what is odd about the genesis block: the reward that cannot be spent, and the headline that dates it to the term of Chancellor Alistair Darling (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). This subject covers Genesis coinbase unspendable; The Chancellor of the headline.

nodes.label: Genesis coinbase unspendable
nodes.body: The 50 coins of the genesis block can never be spent: the Bitcoin Wiki says that this follows from a quirk in the way the genesis block is written in the code, and that it is not known whether it was intended (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). A Bitcoin Core 31.1 node on the test chain confirmed the quirk in three ways: getrawtransaction refused the genesis coinbase with the message that it is not an ordinary transaction, gettxout found no output for it, and the UTXO set at height 0 held 0 outputs (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book is silent on the point, and a student who tries to look the transaction up with the usual tools will be surprised (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like the first coin that a shopkeeper nails to the wall: it is the first takings, it is proudly displayed, and it can never go into the till.

nodes.label: The Chancellor of the headline
nodes.body: The headline in the genesis block speaks of the Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks, and the Chancellor of the Exchequer in office on 3 January 2009 was Alistair Darling, who served under Prime Minister Gordon Brown from 2007 to 2010 (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The newspaper, The Times, began in 1785 under the title The Daily Universal Register and took its modern name on 1 January 1788, so it is a daily with a long record, a respectable witness for a date (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The book points to the headline as proof of the earliest date and as a reminder of the crisis in which Bitcoin was launched (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The timestamp in the genesis header, 2009-01-03 18:15:05 UTC, falls on the same day as the issue. A headline in a block is like the date on a milk carton: it tells you the earliest day the milk could be fresh.

nodes.label: Linking blocks
nodes.body: The fourth section is about the chain itself: how each block commits to its parent, why changing an old block means mining all that follow it, what a fork is and how the odds of a reorganization fall with depth (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The ice core of the book's comparison is checked here as well (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). This subject covers Back links; Forks and reorganizations.

nodes.label: Back links
nodes.body: This subject asks how blocks are linked backward and why that makes history hard to change: the previous-hash field, a real example, the effect of tampering, accumulated work, the old idea of linked time-stamps and the picture of the ice core (Haber and Stornetta, 1991). This subject covers Previous hash points to parent; Links of block 277,315; Tampering breaks descendants; Chain work accumulates; Hash-chained timestamps; Glacier core analogy.

nodes.label: Previous hash points to parent
nodes.body: Each block commits to its parent by carrying the parent's hash in its previous-block field, and that sequence of hashes is the chain that runs back to the genesis block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For ten consecutive headers of the test chain, heights 480 to 489, the code of this chapter recomputed every header's hash and compared it with the previous-block field of the next header: 9 of 9 links agreed (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A full node checks this link for every block it receives, which is how it knows where to attach the block. It is like the page numbers and references in a ledger where each page begins with the closing balance of the page before: a missing or changed page shows at once.

nodes.label: Links of block 277,315
nodes.body: The book's example is a real pair of blocks: a node whose tip is block 277,314 with the hash 00000000000000027e7b... receives a block whose previousblockhash is that value, and so extends the chain to height 277,315 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example therefore holds after more than ten years: a hash does not age. It is like a train whose coupling is checked at each station: the new carriage is accepted only if it fits the one in front. nodes.label: Tampering breaks descendants
nodes.body: Because the previous-block field is part of the header and so of the hash, changing a block changes its own hash and breaks the link in the next block, which would have to be changed and mined again, and so on up to the tip (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the experiment of this chapter one bit of the merkle root of block 483 of the test chain was flipped: the block's own hash changed, the previous-hash link of block 484 no longer matched, and 7 blocks, from 483 to 489, would have to be mined again (Bitcoin Core, 2026). At the difficulty of block 277,315 each of these re-mined blocks would take about 5 x 10^18 hashes, which is the practical meaning of a deep block being safe. It is like a row of dominoes glued edge to edge: you cannot take out one without breaking the glue of all those that stand behind it.

nodes.label: Chain work accumulates
nodes.body: A node does not follow the longest chain but the chain with the most accumulated work, and each header adds the work that its target stands for (Bitcoin Core, 2026). On the test chain, where every block has the bits 0x207fffff, one block is worth 2 units of work, so the chainwork printed by the node was 2, 4, 6 and 8 at heights 0 to 3 and 1002 (0x3ea) after the 501 blocks of the run, exactly 2 x 501; the genesis block of mainnet starts at 0x100010001, as the book's listing shows (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The difference between length and work matters only when difficulty differs between the branches, and that is why the book can say 'longer chain' for the simple case. It is like a tug of war decided by the total strength on each rope and not by the number of people holding it.

nodes.label: Hash-chained timestamps
nodes.body: The idea of linking records by hashes is older than Bitcoin: Stuart Haber and W. Scott Stornetta published How to Time-Stamp a Digital Document in the Journal of Cryptology in 1991, describing how each time-stamp can contain the hash of the one before so that records cannot be inserted or altered afterwards (Haber and Stornetta, 1991). Nakamoto's paper cites their work for the timestamp server on which the block chain is based, and describes how transactions are hashed in a Merkle tree, a structure from Ralph Merkle's work of 1980 on protocols for public-key systems (Nakamoto, 2008); (Merkle, 1980). What the block chain added was a way to agree on the order without a trusted time-stamping office, using proof of work. It is like a notary's book with numbered pages: nothing in it needs to be secret, but a page cannot be slipped in without the numbers showing it. This example reads haber_stornetta_1991_timestamp.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. nodes.label: Glacier core analogy
nodes.body: The book compares the chain to the layers of a glacier or an ice core: the top is loose and may change with the seasons, but a little way down the layers are stable and further down they are a record of millions of years (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The comparison is not far off, because an ice core is built from the incremental buildup of annual layers of snow, the cores at Dome C in Antarctica go back nearly 800,000 years, and cores drilled in 2016 at the Allan Hills held ice up to 2.7 million years old (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). In blocks, the six topsoil blocks are about an hour of work and the 100 blocks of coinbase maturity about 16.7 hours, so the 'millions of years' of the book are meant as a picture and not as a measure, since the whole chain is only about 18.5 years old. It is the same picture as a stack of newspapers in a cellar: today's paper is on top and can be taken off, but nobody can slip an issue into the middle of last year's pile without the whole pile showing it.

nodes.label: Forks and reorganizations
nodes.body: This subject asks what happens when two blocks compete: the fork, the switch to the heavier branch and the fall of the odds of a reorganization with depth (Nakamoto, 2008). This subject covers Two children one parent; Fork resolved by more work; Reorganization probability falls.

nodes.label: Two children one parent
nodes.body: A block has one parent but may have several children, and when two miners find a block at almost the same time the chain forks for a while: two blocks that both commit to the same parent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the test chain this was made to happen on purpose: two blocks with different hashes and the same previous-block field were both at height 511, and the node's getchaintips listed two tips, one active and one of status valid-fork with branch length 1 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A fork is not an error, it is the normal result of two miners racing on a network where messages need time to travel. It is like two people arriving at a till at the same moment: for a second there are two candidates, and then one of them is served first.
nodes.definition: A fork on the test chain: two different blocks with the same parent hash and the same height 511, one active and one a valid-fork branch of length 1.

nodes.label: Fork resolved by more work
nodes.body: A fork is resolved when one branch becomes heavier: nodes switch to the branch with the most accumulated work, and the other branch is kept as a valid-fork that may come back if it is extended later (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the test chain a third block was built on the first child; the tip moved to height 512, the first child's branch became the active chain, and the second child stayed in the list as a valid-fork at height 511 with branch length 1, so nothing was deleted, only passed over (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book calls the situation temporary and says that eventually only one child becomes part of the chain accepted by all full nodes. It is like a road with two lanes that merge: both cars were driving legally, one is waved on first, and the other follows at once behind it.
nodes.definition: A third block on top of the first child made height 512 the tip, the first child's branch active and the second child a valid-fork branch at height 511 of length 1, so the fork was resolved without anyone deleting a block.

nodes.label: Reorganization probability falls
nodes.body: The book says that blocks near the tip may be revised, and that further down they are less and less likely to change until the probability becomes infinitesimal; Nakamoto's paper gives the numbers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Nakamoto, 2008). For an attacker with 10 percent of the hash rate, the chance of ever catching up from 0, 1, 2, 6 and 10 blocks behind is 1.0, 0.2045873, 0.0509779, 0.0002428 and 0.0000012, and for 30 percent at 6 blocks it is 0.1321; the code of this chapter reproduced the paper's table from its Poisson formula to the printed digits. This is the mathematical reason for the habit of waiting six confirmations. It is like the chance of a runner who starts six laps behind to catch up with someone who runs almost as fast as he does: not zero, but small enough to bet against.

nodes.label: Merkle trees
nodes.body: The fifth section teaches the merkle tree that summarizes the transactions of a block in 32 bytes: how it is built, its two known weaknesses and how a short path proves that one transaction is in a block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It has the most executed leaves of the chapter, because every statement about hashes can be recomputed (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Tree construction; Tree flaws; Merkle proofs.

nodes.label: Tree construction
nodes.body: This subject asks how a merkle tree is built: pairs, the duplicated odd hash, a 32-byte root whatever the size, the depth, a real block and the history of the idea (Merkle, 1980). This subject covers Tree of four leaves; Odd leaf duplicated; Root is always32 bytes; Tree depth; Real block root; Hash tree history.

nodes.label: Tree of four leaves
nodes.body: A merkle tree is built from the bottom: each transaction is hashed to give a leaf, and every pair of neighbours is joined (their two 32-byte hashes written one after the other, 64 bytes) and hashed twice again to give the parent, until one hash, the merkle root, is left (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For the block of four transactions on the test chain the code of this chapter hashed the pairs by hand, H_AB = SHA256(SHA256(H_A || H_B)) and H_CD likewise, then the pair of those, and the result equalled the merkle root in the block's header, with levels of 4, 2 and 1 hashes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The same method is described in the Bitcoin developer guide with the letters A to E (Bitcoin Project, 2026). Think of a knockout tournament: the players are the leaves, each match produces a winner, and the champion at the top stands for the whole field.
nodes.definition: A block with four transactions has a tree of 4, 2 and 1 hashes: H_AB = SHA256(SHA256(H_A || H_B)) and H_CD likewise, and the double hash of H_AB || H_CD equalled the merkle root in the header of the test chain's block.

nodes.label: Odd leaf duplicated
nodes.body: When a level has an odd number of hashes, the last one is paired with itself, so that the tree stays balanced; the book shows this for three transactions, where transaction C is duplicated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the test chain the block with three transactions had levels of 3, 2 and 1 hashes, the root h(h(A||B) || h(C||C)) equalled the header's merkle root, and the same rule reproduced the root of all eight blocks with 1 to 8 transactions (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The developer guide draws the same picture with E paired with itself (Bitcoin Project, 2026). The rule is simple and has a price, which the section on the design flaw shows. It is like a football draw with an odd number of teams, in which one team plays a 'match' against its own shadow and moves on.

nodes.label: Root is always32 bytes
nodes.body: However many transactions a block holds, its summary in the header is a single 32-byte hash, because a hash always has the same length (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The test chain's blocks of 1, 2, 8 and 16 transactions all have a 32-byte root, block 840,000 with its 3,050 transactions has a root of 32 bytes too (031b417c...), and for a block with a single transaction the root is that transaction's id: the genesis block's merkle root 4a5e1e4b... is the id of its only transaction (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This is the strength of a commitment: the header can stay small and the data behind it can grow. It is like the barcode on a pack, which has the same width whether the pack holds a single biscuit or a whole case. nodes.label: Tree depth
nodes.body: The depth of a merkle tree, the number of hashing steps from a leaf to the root, is the ceiling of the base-2 logarithm of the number of leaves, so proving that one transaction is included takes about log2(N) hashes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The code gave depths of 0 for 1 transaction, 2 for 4, 4 for 16, 6 for the 40 transactions of block 277,315, 12 for the 3,050 of block 840,000 and 14 for 16,000, and building the real tree of block 277,315 level by level gave exactly 6 steps (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A logarithm grows so slowly that doubling the size of a block adds only one step. It is like finding a name in a phone book by opening in the middle each time: a book ten times as thick needs only about three more openings. This example reads mempool_txids_277315.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. nodes.label: Real block root
nodes.body: The strongest test of the construction is a real block: mempool.space lists the 40 transaction ids of block 277,315, from 257e7497... to 05cfd38f..., and the merkle root computed from them with the rule of the book is 5e049f40..., the value in the block's header and in the book's listing (Mempool Space, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The code does nothing but the pairing and double hashing of the chapter, with the ids taken in their internal byte order (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The result holds for a block mined in December 2013 as it does for one mined today. It is like checking a sum of forty receipts: if the total at the bottom of the page is right, then every receipt that was added must be among them. nodes.label: Hash tree history
nodes.body: The hash tree is named after Ralph Merkle, who patented it in 1979; the patent, US 4309569 'Method of providing digital signatures', was published on 5 January 1982 and assigned to Stanford University, and it explains both the tree and its use for many one-time signatures (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). Merkle wrote about tree authentication for public file directories in his paper Protocols for Public Key Cryptosystems of 1980 (Merkle, 1980). Nakamoto's paper uses the tree to let old blocks be compressed by discarding the interior hashes of the tree, so only the root remains in the header (Nakamoto, 2008). The tree is like a company's organization chart: the chief executive need not know every employee, only the few managers who each answer for a branch. nodes.label: Tree flaws
nodes.body: This subject asks where the construction is weak: the duplicated hash that lets two lists have one root, the defence in the code, the run that shows it, and the 64-byte transaction that looks like an inner node (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). This subject covers CVE-2012-2459 trees; Node rejects mutated block; Mutation defence in the source; The 64-byte weakness.

nodes.label: CVE-2012-2459 trees
nodes.body: The rule that an odd last hash is duplicated has a consequence that a comment in the source calls a serious flaw: different lists of transactions can have the same merkle root (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's example is the lists [1,2,3,4,5,6] and [1,2,3,4,5,6,5,6], and the code of this chapter reproduced it with six dummy ids: the roots are equal although the lists have 6 and 8 entries; [1,2,3] and [1,2,3,3] also agree, whereas [1,2,3,4] and [1,2,3,4,3,4] do not, because the duplication only works at the end of a level that is odd. A block with the longer list has the same header and the same block hash but is invalid, and Optech's description is that a node that stored the invalid form's hash as bad would refuse the good block from everybody (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). It is like a cashier who, to save time, counts the last odd coin twice: a customer can hand in an extra coin pair that changes nothing in the total.
nodes.definition: The lists of six and of eight transaction ids [1,2,3,4,5,6] and [1,2,3,4,5,6,5,6] have the same merkle root, and so do [1,2,3] and [1,2,3,3], but [1,2,3,4] and [1,2,3,4,3,4] do not: the duplication of an odd last hash can be forged.

nodes.label: Node rejects mutated block
nodes.body: Because the mutated block has the same hash as the original, a careless node could remember that hash as bad and then refuse the good block (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). Bitcoin Core avoids it, and the test chain showed how: a block of 3 transactions was changed into one of 4 by repeating the last transaction, with the header unchanged and the same hash; submitblock answered bad-txns-duplicate, the node still did not know the block afterwards (getblockheader said Block not found), and when the original block was submitted afterwards it was accepted and became the tip (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The attack would have let someone feed a node a doctored copy and keep it from learning the true block, a form of the eclipse attack. It is like a post office that returns a forged parcel to the sender but does not blacklist the address: the real parcel with the same label is still delivered when it arrives.
nodes.definition: A block of 3 transactions was changed into one of 4 by repeating the last transaction, with the same header and the same hash: submitblock answered bad-txns-duplicate, and the original block was then accepted and became the tip, so the invalid form did not block the valid one.

nodes.label: Mutation defence in the source
nodes.body: The defence is written into the code: merkle.cpp warns against the flaw in its comment and its root function reports through a mutated flag when two identical hashes meet at the end of a level, and validation.cpp turns this into the result BLOCK_MUTATED with the reason bad-txns-duplicate (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book reproduces the comment, with slight revisions, in a box (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Optech's timeline is that the vulnerability was reported in 2012, assigned the number CVE-2012-2459 and fixed quietly without being exploited as far as is known, that a variation was reintroduced in version 0.13.0 of 2016 and fixed in 0.14.0, and that another variation was found and fixed in 2023 (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). A bug of this kind is like a hole that is closed in the fence and then reopens when the fence is rebuilt, which is why a good comment stays in the code.
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core's merkle.cpp warns of CVE-2012-2459 and reports a mutated block, validation.cpp rejects it as bad-txns-duplicate (the run showed the genuine block accepted afterwards), and Optech dates the report to 2012 and a variation to version 0.13.0 of 2016.

nodes.label: The 64-byte weakness
nodes.body: The tree has a second weakness: an inner node is the hash of exactly 64 bytes, two child hashes side by side, and a transaction whose serialization without witness data is exactly 64 bytes can be mistaken for an inner node (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025). The code showed the size, 2 x 32 = 64 bytes for the inner node of the test chain's block, and the smallest transaction is 60 bytes (a weight of 240), so a 64-byte transaction is only four bytes above the minimum and can exist (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Optech names this weakness CVE-2017-12842, discovered in 2017, and BIP 54 of the consensus cleanup proposal closes it by making such transactions invalid (Bitcoin Optech, 2026); (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025). A light client that checks a merkle path is the one at risk, because it cannot see the whole block. It is like a counterfeit note printed to the size of a wage envelope: at a glance the envelope and the note are the same thing.

nodes.label: Merkle proofs
nodes.body: This subject asks how inclusion is proved with a short path: the path of the 11th of 16 transactions, its logarithmic length, the size compared with a block, the merkleblock message and the importance of left and right (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers Merkle path of 16 transactions; Path length logarithm; Proof size vs block; Merkleblock for light clients; Merkle proof direction.

nodes.label: Merkle path of 16 transactions
nodes.body: To prove that one transaction is in a block, a node does not send the whole block but a merkle path: the one sibling hash at every level of the tree, so that the checker can recompute the root (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's example is transaction K among 16, a path of four hashes, H_L, H_IJ, H_MNOP and H_ABCDEFGH, 128 bytes; the block of 16 transactions on the test chain gave the same thing for its 11th transaction, index 10: a path of 4 hashes with the siblings on the right, left, right and left, and following it reproduced the merkle root in the header (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Bitcoin Core's own gettxoutproof for that transaction verified with verifytxoutproof. It is like proving that you belong to a family by showing a chain of cousins' names instead of the whole family album.
nodes.example: K of 16: L, IJ, MNOP, ABCDEFGH
nodes.definition: For the 11th of 16 transactions (index 10, the K of the book's figure) the path has 4 hashes, 128 bytes, with the siblings on the right, left, right and left, and following it gave the merkle root of the test chain's 16-transaction block.

nodes.label: Path length logarithm
nodes.body: The size of a path grows with the logarithm, not with the count of transactions: a block of 1,024 transactions needs 10 hashes (320 bytes), 4,096 needs 12 (384 bytes) and 16,000 needs 14 (448 bytes), the numbers behind the book's statement of paths of 10 or 12 hashes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The code checked these, and a path through the real tree of block 277,315, which has 40 transactions, had 6 hashes, 192 bytes (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A thousand transactions are therefore proved by a few hundred bytes. It is like the questions in the game of twenty questions: with ten questions that cut the field in half each time you can single out one of a thousand. This example reads mempool_txids_277315.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: ([(1024, 10, 320), (4096, 12, 384), (16000, 14, 448)], 6, True)
nodes.definition: A path for 1,024 transactions has 10 hashes (320 bytes), for 4,096 has 12 (384 bytes) and for 16,000 has 14 (448 bytes), and block 277,315 with 40 transactions needs 6.

nodes.label: Proof size vs block
nodes.body: The book closes the section by saying that the largest possible proof is almost 10,000 times smaller than the largest block, but the numbers do not quite support this (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A proof needs the 80-byte header and 448 bytes of path, 528 bytes, and a block of 4,000,000 bytes is 7,576 times larger than that; if the transaction itself, say 250 bytes, is counted as the book says, the ratio is 5,141; to reach 10,000 the proof would have to be 400 bytes, less than the header and the path together. The idea of the book is right and the factor is overstated by about a third against the header and path alone and by almost double with a typical transaction, an erratum of arithmetic and not of principle. It is like saying that a postcard is ten thousand times lighter than a parcel when it is in fact five or seven thousand times: the point that it is far lighter stands.
nodes.definition: A proof of 80 + 448 = 528 bytes is 7,576 times smaller than a block of 4,000,000 bytes, and with a typical 250-byte transaction added 5,141 times smaller, so the book's 'almost 10,000 times' would need a proof of 400 bytes.

io.code: (round(4000000 / (80 + 448)), round(4000000 / (250 + 80 + 448)), 4000000 // 10000, L.has('book_ch11_blockchain.adoc', 'almost 10,000 times smaller'))

nodes.label: Merkleblock for light clients
nodes.body: A lightweight client does not download blocks; it receives a merkleblock message, which holds the header and a merkle path to the transaction it asked for, and with the header it checks that the transaction is in the block and the block is in the chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's gettxoutproof makes such a message, and on the test chain the one for a transaction of the block with 16 transactions was 248 bytes (80 of header, the count 16, 5 hashes, 2 bytes of flags) against 3,580 bytes for the block, verified by verifytxoutproof; for a block of 4 transactions it was 183 bytes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book states that the client receives less than a kilobyte, more than a thousand times less than the block of about 2 MB; block 840,000 had 2,325,617 bytes (Mempool Space, 2026). The book ties this to Bloom filters, which Bitcoin Core now keeps off by default, so a client today gets the proof by other means. It is like a receipt with a stamp: a small piece of paper that proves a purchase without the whole shop's accounts.
nodes.definition: The merkleblock that Bitcoin Core made for one transaction of the test chain's 16-transaction block was 248 bytes (header, count 16, 5 hashes, flags) against the block's 3,580 bytes, and verifytxoutproof returned the transaction; for a block of 4 transactions it was 183 bytes.

nodes.label: Merkle proof direction
nodes.body: A merkle path is not just a list of hashes: it also matters on which side each sibling lies, because the double hash of A||B is not that of B||A (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The sides are given by the position of the transaction: for the transaction at index 10, binary 1010, the lowest bit 0 means that the node is a left child and its sibling is on the right, the next bit 1 that the sibling is on the left, and so on, so the sides run right, left, right, left. The code followed the path with the right sides and recovered the root of the test chain's block, and with the sides swapped it did not (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like the two halves of a handshake password: the same words in the wrong order do not open the door.
nodes.definition: The order of every pair matters: following the path with the right sides swapped did not give the root, and the sides are the bits of the transaction's position, 1010 read from the lowest bit for index 10.

nodes.label: Test blockchains
nodes.body: The sixth section is about the chains on which Bitcoin software can be tried without risk: testnet, signet and regtest, with their genesis blocks, addresses, difficulty rules and sizes, and the pipeline from one to the next (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is the section where the book is most out of date, because testnet4 and the end of testnet3 came after it (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024). This subject covers Chains and addresses; Testnet; Signet; Regtest; Development pipeline.

nodes.label: Chains and addresses
nodes.body: This subject asks which chains exist and how they are kept apart: genesis blocks, address prefixes, data directories and the sizes of the chains (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Several chains exist; Address prefixes; Data directories; Assumed chain sizes.

nodes.label: Several chains exist
nodes.body: There is not one Bitcoin blockchain but several: the main chain created on 3 January 2009 is called mainnet, and the book names three more that exist for testing, testnet, signet and regtest (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core 31.1 lists the chains main, test, testnet4, signet and regtest in the help of the option -chain, and the nodes of this chapter started on each of them reported genesis hashes that equal the ones the code rebuilt from chainparams.cpp: 000000000933ea01... for testnet3, 00000000da84f2ba... for testnet4, 00000008819873e9... for signet and 0f9188f1... for regtest (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). Each chain has its own genesis block, its own message-start bytes on the network and its own data directory, so the chains cannot be mixed up. It is like the different currencies in a board game: the notes look alike, but the ones from the box of one game are not accepted in the box of another.
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core 31.1 knows five chains, main, test, testnet4, signet and regtest, and the genesis hashes that the nodes reported for testnet3, testnet4, signet and regtest equal those rebuilt from chainparams.cpp.

nodes.label: Address prefixes
nodes.body: The test chains use other address prefixes than mainnet so that nobody sends real coins to a test address by mistake (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the source the base58 prefixes are 0 and 5 on mainnet (addresses starting with 1 and 3) and 111 and 196 on the test chains (starting with m or n, and with 2), while the bech32 prefix is bc on mainnet, tb on testnet3, testnet4 and signet, and bcrt on regtest (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The nodes of this chapter produced exactly these: legacy addresses beginning with m, script addresses with 2, tb1q for segwit and tb1p for taproot on testnet4 and signet, and bcrt1q and bcrt1p on regtest. The book's tip lists m, n and tb1 and so leaves out the prefix 2 of script addresses and the bcrt1 of regtest, which its own regtest listing uses a few pages later (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The prefix is like the country code of a telephone number: you know at once that the number is not for a local call.
nodes.definition: The test chains share the base58 prefixes 111 (addresses starting m or n) and 196 (starting 2) and the bech32 prefix tb, with tb1q for segwit and tb1p for taproot, while regtest uses bcrt1q and bcrt1p, so the book's list of m, n and tb1 leaves out the 2 and the regtest prefix that its own listing uses.

nodes.label: Data directories
nodes.body: Bitcoin Core keeps each chain apart in its own subdirectory of the data directory, so that a developer can run mainnet and a test chain on one machine: regtest, testnet3, testnet4 and signet, with the main chain in the directory itself (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The nodes of the run reported the data directories regtest, testnet4, signet and testnet3, matching the book's examples for testnet3 and regtest, and each chain has its own default port: 8333 for mainnet, 18333 for testnet3, 48333 for testnet4, 38333 for signet and 18444 for regtest (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). Separate directories and ports mean that a mistake with one chain cannot damage another. It is like having a separate drawer in the kitchen for each kind of cutlery: the knives are all in the house, but you do not reach for them when you want a spoon.
nodes.definition: Each chain keeps its data in its own subdirectory, regtest, testnet3, testnet4 and signet, and uses its own port: 8333, 18333, 48333, 38333 and 18444.

nodes.label: Assumed chain sizes
nodes.body: The book says that testnet3 was a large blockchain, in excess of 30 GB in 2023, and that the default signet was about a gigabyte in size, with a listing showing size_on_disk 769,525,915 bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core keeps an estimate of each chain's size for the warning about free disk space, and in the release 31.1 source the estimates are 856 GB for mainnet, 245 GB for testnet3, 31 GB for testnet4 and 24 GB for the default signet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). These figures are approximate, but they show that testnet3 is about eight times larger than the book's lower bound and that the signet has grown to about 31 times the size in the book's listing, as one would expect from the chain having more than doubled in blocks. A test chain called light can therefore need a lot of disk space, and the cheapest test environment remains regtest, which starts at zero. It is like a spare room that was meant to hold a few boxes and now holds the stock of a shop.

nodes.label: Testnet
nodes.body: This subject asks about the public proof-of-work test network: testnet3, which is deprecated, testnet4 that replaces it, the minimum-difficulty rule, the block storms and the two rules of BIP 94 (Jahr, 2024). This subject covers Testnet3 is still there; Testnet4 replaces testnet3; Testnet minimum difficulty; Testnet block storms; BIP 94 rules.

nodes.label: Testnet3 is still there
nodes.body: The book says that the current testnet is testnet3, restarted in February 2011 to reset the difficulty (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core 31.1 still starts it with the option -testnet, reporting the chain name test and the data directory testnet3, and the chain created on 2011-02-02 stood on 2026-10-15 at height 5,189,394, but the help text of the option says that support for testnet3 is deprecated and will be removed in an upcoming release, and recommends testnet4 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026). Release 28.0 had already announced the intention to phase testnet3 out (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024). So the book's sentence is still true of the code but no longer of the advice. It is like an old road that is still on the map and drivable, with a sign at the entrance telling you to take the new bypass. This example reads mempool_testnet3_tip_height.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: ('test', ['testnet3'], '2011-02-02', True, 5189394, True)

nodes.label: Testnet4 replaces testnet3
nodes.body: Testnet4 is the replacement for testnet3, specified in BIP 94 by Fabian Jahr, assigned on 2024-05-27 and now Deployed, and supported in Bitcoin Core since release 28.0 with the option -testnet4 (Jahr, 2024); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024). Its genesis block carries the message 03/May/2024 followed by a 64-digit hexadecimal number in the form of a block hash, has the hash 00000000da84f2ba..., the time 2024-05-03 23:11:00 UTC, and the chain stood on 2026-10-15 at height 156,618, where testnet3 had 5,189,394 (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026). Optech reports that the testnet is a testing network included with Bitcoin Core and supported by many other programs, with testnet4 a recently started replacement (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). A new test chain is like a new notebook after the old one has been scribbled all over: the same pen, a clean page. This example reads mempool_testnet4_tip_height.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: ('00000000da84f2ba', '03/May/2024 000000000000000000001ebd58c244970b3aa9d783bb001011fbe8ea8e98e00e', '2024-05-03 23:11:00', 156618, True, True)
nodes.definition: Testnet4 begins with a genesis block that quotes the Bitcoin block hash of 3 May 2024, hash 00000000da84f2ba..., time 2024-05-03 23:11:00 UTC, added to Bitcoin Core in release 28.0 by BIP 94, and it stood on 2026-10-15 at height 156,618.

nodes.label: Testnet minimum difficulty
nodes.body: The book says that testnet's minimum difficulty is half that of Bitcoin and that a block may be mined at the minimum difficulty if its timestamp is more than 20 minutes after the previous one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second half is right in the code: in pow.cpp a testnet block whose time is later than the previous block's time plus 2 x nPowTargetSpacing, 2 x 10 minutes, must use the minimum difficulty, and the flag is true for testnet3, testnet4 and regtest and false for mainnet and signet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The first half does not show in chainparams.cpp, where mainnet and testnet3 have the same powLimit 00000000ffff...; the sentence matches the Bitcoin Wiki, which says that the minimum difficulty of 1.0 on testnet equals 0.5 on mainnet, but the code gives no support for such a factor (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). It is a small imprecision that the book has taken over from a secondary source. The 20-minute exception is like a quiet night rule at a pool: when nobody has swum for a while, anyone may get in the water without the usual test.
nodes.definition: The code lets testnet3, testnet4 and regtest (not mainnet, not signet) mine a block at the minimum difficulty when its time is more than 2 x 10 = 20 minutes after the previous block; the book's 'half that of Bitcoin' does not show in the code, in which mainnet and testnet3 have the same limit 00000000ffff.....

nodes.label: Testnet block storms
nodes.body: The book describes disruptive miners who create many blocks in a row on testnet without transactions and make it unusable (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The numbers show the damage: testnet3 had 5,189,394 blocks on 2026-10-15, 6.3 times the 825,696 that one block in ten minutes since 2011-02-02 would have given, and more than 5 times the 971,537 blocks of mainnet; BIP 94 says that three years' worth of blocks were mined in a few weeks and the network was practically unusable (Mempool Space, 2026); (Jahr, 2024). The Bitcoin Wiki dates the blog post of Jameson Lopp, Griefing Bitcoin's Testnet, to 4 May 2024 and calls it the catalyst for testnet4 (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). A block storm is like a faucet that someone has left open in a rented flat: the minimum-difficulty rule is meant for a trickle, and the tenant upstairs turns it into a flood. This example reads mempool_testnet3_tip_height.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: (5189394, 825696, 6.3, 971537, True)

nodes.label: BIP 94 rules
nodes.body: BIP 94 changes two rules for testnet4 and keeps the 20-minute exception for CPU mining: the difficulty adjustment takes its base from the first block of the previous period instead of the last, which stops a minimum-difficulty block at the end of a period from resetting the whole next period, and the first block of each period of 2016 blocks may not have a time more than 600 seconds before its parent's (Jahr, 2024). Bitcoin Core switches the rule on by the parameter enforce_BIP94, which only testnet4 sets, and the code of pow.cpp starts the retarget from pindexFirst->nBits when it is set (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Release 29.0 made the timewarp rule inactive on regtest and made block templates respect it on all networks, so miners are ready if mainnet adopts a timewarp fix (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025). The timewarp rule comes from the consensus cleanup proposal that Optech describes (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). It is like a speed limit that is first tried on a quiet side road, and written into the main road code later if it works.
nodes.definition: BIP 94 changes two rules for testnet4: the retarget starts from the first block of the previous period, and the first block of a period may be no more than 600 seconds earlier than its parent; the code switches this on with enforce_BIP94, which only testnet4 sets, and release 29.0 switched the timewarp rule off for regtest.

nodes.label: Signet
nodes.body: This subject asks about the signed test network: the challenge script, the message start derived from it, the shared genesis block and the growth of the default signet (Alm and Towns, 2019). This subject covers Signet challenge is a multisig; Signet message start from the challenge; Signet genesis shared; Signet size today.

nodes.label: Signet challenge is a multisig
nodes.body: A signet is a test network in which every block must carry a solution to a challenge script, a normal Bitcoin script, so that only the holder of the keys can make blocks, which is why the book calls it fully permissioned (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Alm and Towns, 2019). The challenge of the default signet in Bitcoin Core 31.1 is 71 bytes long and disassembles to OP_1, two public keys of 33 bytes, OP_2 and OP_CHECKMULTISIG, a 1-of-2 multisig: either of the two operators can sign, as the book says that two contributors operate the default signet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The custom signet of the run used the challenge 51, a single OP_1, which anyone can satisfy, so it is a signet in name only. The Optech topic explains that signed blocks give the creator complete control over the test network (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). It is like a theatre where only people with a ticket stub from one of two box offices can walk on the stage, however many people want to try.
nodes.definition: The default signet's challenge is a 71-byte script, OP_1 followed by two 33-byte keys and OP_2 OP_CHECKMULTISIG, so a block needs the signature of one of the two operators, while the custom signet of the run used the one-byte challenge 51 (OP_1), which anyone can satisfy.

nodes.label: Signet message start from the challenge
nodes.body: Peers must not mistake one signet for another, so the four message-start bytes of a signet are not fixed in the source but computed: they are the first four bytes of the double SHA-256 of the challenge script with its length in front (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The code of this chapter reproduced the rule on three challenges: 0a03cf40 for the default signet, 54d26fbd for the one-byte challenge 51, and 7ec653a5 for the example given in BIP 325, the very value the BIP lists as the message start (Alm and Towns, 2019). A custom signet therefore needs no registry of magic numbers: choosing a new challenge chooses a new network. It is like a secret handshake derived from the club's password: change the password and all the hands change.
nodes.definition: The four message-start bytes of a signet are the first four bytes of the double SHA-256 of its challenge: 0a03cf40 for the default signet, 54d26fbd for the challenge 51, and 7ec653a5 for the example of BIP 325, so two signets do not talk to each other by mistake.

nodes.label: Signet genesis shared
nodes.body: All signets start from the same genesis block, whatever their challenge: the default signet and the custom signet with the challenge 51 in the run both reported the hash 000000088198..., the time 2020-09-01 00:00:00 UTC and the bits 1e0377ae, because the genesis block does not contain the challenge (Bitcoin Core, 2026). What separates one signet from another is therefore the challenge and the blocks that follow it, and the message-start bytes derived from it. BIP 325 was assigned to Karl-Johan Alm and Anthony Towns on 2019-03-20, and Bitcoin Core 0.21.0 added the support, with one public signet maintained and personal signets possible (Alm and Towns, 2019); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2021). It is like a set of identical blank forms from one printer: the forms are the same, and it is the stamp that makes each club's version its own.

nodes.label: Signet size today
nodes.body: The book says that the default signet has about 150,000 blocks and gives a listing with 143,619 blocks and 769 megabytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On 2026-10-15 the tip of the default signet was at height 326,440, 2.27 times as many, close to the 321,840 that one block in ten minutes since the genesis of 2020-09-01 would give, so the signet keeps its target pace (Mempool Space, 2026). The book adds that the default signet is used to test proposed upgrades through the Bitcoin Inquisition project, and a signet can show a demonstration, as Optech notes for the slow blocks of BIP 54 (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). The book's figures are therefore a snapshot of 2023, not a property of the network. A number like this is a photograph of a growing child: true on the day it was taken. This example reads mempool_signet_tip_height.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: (326440, 2.27, 321840, True)

nodes.label: Regtest
nodes.body: This subject asks about the private test chain that the reader can run: its start state, the halving every 150 blocks, the balance after 500 blocks and the wallet command of the book that no longer works (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Regtest start state; Regtest halves every 150 blocks; Regtest balance after 500 blocks; No default wallet.

nodes.label: Regtest start state
nodes.body: Regtest, short for regression testing, is a chain that exists only on your own machine: you launch it from scratch, with no other node unless you add one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A fresh Bitcoin Core 31.1 node on regtest reported the chain regtest, 0 blocks, 0 headers, the difficulty 4.656542373906925e-10, the median time 1296688602 and the best block hash 0f9188f13cb7b2c71f2a335e3a4fc328bf5beb436012afca590b1a11466e2206, exactly the values in the book's listing, including the chainwork ending in 02 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The difficulty is so low because the target 7fff... lets about every second hash win. It is like a driving school's empty car park: the rules of the road are the same, but you can practise a hundred times without meeting anybody.

nodes.label: Regtest halves every 150 blocks
nodes.body: On mainnet the block reward halves every 210,000 blocks, about four years; on regtest the interval is only 150, so that a developer can see several halvings within a few minutes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The test chain showed the reward through getblockstats: 50 coins at heights 1 and 149, 25 at 150 and 299, 12.5 at 300 and 449, and 6.25 at 450 and 500, the same values as the code's subsidy rule with the interval 150 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book does not mention the interval, but it leads to the balance in the next listing. It is like a kitchen timer that is set to seconds instead of hours so that a lesson on 'cooking times' fits in a class.
nodes.definition: The reward on regtest halves every 150 blocks instead of every 210,000: 50 coins for heights 1 to 149, 25 from 150, 12.5 from 300 and 6.25 from 450.
