nodes.label: Regtest balance after 500 blocks
nodes.body: The book mines 500 blocks on regtest and finds a balance of 12,462.5 coins, because the rewards must be 100 blocks deep to be spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The sums agree: the rewards of blocks 1 to 400 add up to 149 x 50 + 150 x 25 + 101 x 12.5 = 12,462.5, the 100 blocks 401 to 500 gave 931.25 coins that the wallet still showed as immature, and mining the 500 blocks took 2.27 seconds on the shared machine of this run (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's number is correct, and it is correct only because of the interval of 150. It is like a pay slip with a month's wages held back: the full amount is on the paper, but only the older part can be drawn.
nodes.definition: After 500 blocks the wallet showed 12462.5 coins as spendable and 931.25 as immature, which the sums of the halving rewards of blocks 1 to 400 and 401 to 500 give, as in the book; mining the 500 blocks took 2.27 seconds in this run.

nodes.label: No default wallet
nodes.body: The book's regtest session begins with the command createwallet with an empty name, to make a default wallet, but a Bitcoin Core 31.1 node refuses it: the command printed the error 'Wallet name cannot be empty' and exited with code 8 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A fresh node has no wallet at all, listwallets returned an empty list and getnewaddress answered that no wallet is loaded, so a reader who types the commands of the book gets an error at the first step and has to give the wallet a name, for example createwallet test. Release 31.0 mentions the empty wallet name in a different place, the Restore Wallet dialog of the graphical interface, which shows an error if the name is empty (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). It is like a recipe that tells you to use the cupboard with no label: the shop no longer sells cupboards without labels.

nodes.label: Development pipeline
nodes.body: This subject asks how the test chains are used together: from regtest to signet or testnet and then to mainnet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers Pipeline order.

nodes.label: Pipeline order
nodes.body: The book recommends a development pipeline: test the code on regtest, then on signet or testnet, and finally put it into production on mainnet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The source shows how the stages differ in how public they are: regtest has one dummy seed and no peers, signet has 2 DNS seeds and a block rule that needs a signature, testnet3 has 5 seeds and the minimum-difficulty rule, and mainnet has 8 seeds and no such rule (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A developer meets more and more of the real world at each step, other software, other people's transactions and network delays. It is like learning to drive: first the empty car park, then a quiet road with an instructor, and then the motorway.
nodes.definition: The three stages differ in what the code gives them: regtest has one dummy seed and no public peers, signet 2 seeds and a signed block rule, testnet3 5 seeds and the minimum-difficulty rule, mainnet 8 seeds, the order the book recommends.

findings: Background

The chapter describes the blockchain as an ordered, back-linked list of blocks in which every block commits to its parent through the previous-block hash of its header (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The description is confirmed by a real pair of blocks: block 277,315 has the parent hash of block 277,314, version 2, time 1388185038, nonce 4215469401 and merkle root 5e049f40..., the values of the book's listing, with 40 transactions in 43,560 bytes (Mempool Space, 2026). The block hash is the one-line double SHA-256 of the 80-byte header in the code (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Background

The header is 80 bytes and a block may be 4,000,000 bytes, so a block can be 50,000 times the size of its header, as the book says (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); the constant MAX_BLOCK_SERIALIZED_SIZE is 4,000,000 and the header class has the six fields in the order of the book's table (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Today the 971,538 headers of the main chain take about 78 megabytes at 80 bytes each, against a whole chain of 775,272 megabytes (Blockchain Charts, 2026).
Comparative analysis

Erratum of arithmetic: the book says that the largest possible merkle proof is almost 10,000 times smaller than the largest block. The proof needs the 80-byte header and 448 bytes of path, 528 bytes, so a block of 4,000,000 bytes is 7,576 times larger; with a typical 250-byte transaction the ratio is 5,141, and 10,000 would need a proof of 400 bytes. The statement that a path has 10 to 14 hashes (320 to 448 bytes) is right (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The design flaw in the merkle tree is real and has a history: the comment in merkle.cpp warns of CVE-2012-2459, Optech states that the vulnerability was reported in 2012 and fixed quietly, that a variation was reintroduced in 0.13.0 in 2016 and fixed in 0.14.0, and that another was found in 2023; on the test chain a block with a repeated last transaction had the same header and hash and was rejected as bad-txns-duplicate, after which the genuine block was accepted (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The book does not mention the second weakness of the tree: an inner node is the hash of 64 bytes, and a transaction of exactly 64 bytes without witness data can be mistaken for one, which Optech lists as CVE-2017-12842. BIP 54, the consensus cleanup, would make such transactions invalid, which fixes the weakness for light clients without a workaround (Bitcoin Optech, 2026); (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The weight limit is the real block limit: MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT is 4,000,000 weight units and block 840,000 held 3,993,281 weight units in 2,325,617 bytes. Block templates of Bitcoin Core stop at 3,992,000 because 8,000 units are reserved (-blockreservedweight), and release 29.0 fixed a bug that had reserved the 4,000 units twice. The book says that transactions can total about 4,000,000 bytes (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Changed output: the getblock listing of the book has no target and no coinbase_tx. Bitcoin Core 29.0 added the field target to getblock and getblockheader and 31.0 added the coinbase_tx object, and the genesis block of the test chain showed both (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The version field is no longer a version number: BIP 9 requires the top three bits 001 for blocks that signal, giving the range from 0x20000000, and the draft BIP 320 reserves sixteen bits (mask 0x1fffe000) for general use, with BIP 323 proposed as its replacement. Block 840,000 carries 0x2a5fe000 and the blocks of the test chain 0x20000000, while the book says only that the field's use has evolved (Wuille et al., 2015); (BtcDrak, 2018); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Timewarp and testnet storms have shaped recent releases. BIP 94 for testnet4 starts the retarget from the first block of the previous period and bounds the time of the first block of a period to 600 seconds before its parent; Bitcoin Core 29.0 made block templates respect the timewarp rule on all networks and turned the rule off on regtest, and the consensus cleanup of BIP 54 would apply a timewarp fix to mainnet, which Optech's time warp topic explains (Jahr, 2024); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The genesis block holds a first reward that can never be spent, a quirk that the Bitcoin Wiki says may or may not have been intended, and a node on the test chain confirmed that getrawtransaction refuses the genesis coinbase, gettxout returns nothing and the UTXO set at height 0 is empty. Testnet4 has its own genesis coinbase (180 bytes, id 7aa0a7ae...) with the message 03/May/2024; the book does not mention either point (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Jahr, 2024); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The timestamp is described by the book only as an approximate time. The rules are that it must be greater than the median of the previous 11 blocks (BIP 113) and not more than 2 hours ahead of the node's clock, and a 4-byte counter overflows on 2106-02-07; block 277,315 is 1,651 seconds later than its median time past (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Kerin and Friedenbach, 2015); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026); (Wikipedia contributors, 2026).
Comparative analysis

Heights have moved: the book reports height 800,000 in mid 2023, and on 2026-10-15 the main chain was at height 971,537; block 840,000, mined on 2024-04-20 at 00:09:27 UTC, is the first with the reward of 3.125 coins. The book's number of 12,462.5 coins after 500 blocks on regtest is right, because the regtest reward halves every 150 blocks and not every 210,000 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Conclusion

The ideas under the chapter are older than Bitcoin: Haber and Stornetta described hash-linked time-stamping in 1991, Ralph Merkle patented the hash tree in 1979 and described tree authentication in 1980, and Nakamoto's paper cites the first and uses the second for compressing old blocks (Haber and Stornetta, 1991); (Wikipedia contributors, 2026); (Merkle, 1980); (Nakamoto, 2008).
Conclusion

The probability that an attacker with 10 percent of the hash rate catches up from 6 blocks behind is 0.0002428, from 1 block behind 0.2045873, and with 30 percent at 6 blocks 0.1321, computed again with the formula of the paper; this is the quantitative reason behind the book's picture of stable layers (Nakamoto, 2008); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Conclusion

Taken together, the chapter's account of the block, the chain and the merkle tree stands, and every structural claim could be recomputed. What is wrong or out of date lies at the edges: one arithmetic ratio, one sentence on testnet difficulty, the sizes and heights of 2023, the list of address prefixes, the testnet3 advice, the empty wallet name, and five changes of default or output since the book: XOR block files, testnet4, new getblock fields, signet magic by challenge and the reserved block weight (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Erratum for a reader who types the book's regtest session: the first command, createwallet with an empty name, is refused by Bitcoin Core 31.1 with the error 'Wallet name cannot be empty' (exit code 8), a fresh node has no wallet, and getnewaddress fails with 'No wallet is loaded'; the wallet needs a name (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Changed default: since release 28.0 the block files blk*.dat are scrambled with a random XOR key kept in blocks/xor.dat, and older releases and external software cannot read such a directory. In the run the first bytes of blk00000.dat were unreadable until the key d462ed9f917fe79d was applied, after which the file began with the magic fabfb5da and the size 285 of the genesis block. The book describes the blocks as plain data in the files (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Contemporary developments

The book's block table begins with a 4-byte block size, which is not part of a block as it travels or as consensus sees it but a field that Bitcoin Core writes in front of each block in its block files, after the magic bytes; on the test chain the genesis block took 293 bytes on disk, 285 plus 8 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Changed state: the book names testnet3 as the current testnet, but Bitcoin Core 28.0 added testnet4 as specified in BIP 94 (assigned 2024-05-27 to Fabian Jahr, now Deployed), and Bitcoin Core 31.1 still starts testnet3 with -testnet while its help text says that the support is deprecated and will be removed; Optech calls testnet4 a recently started replacement (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Jahr, 2024); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Erratum of size: the book calls testnet3 a chain in excess of 30 GB, but Bitcoin Core 31.1 assumes 245 GB for it in chainparams.cpp, and on 2026-10-15 testnet3 stood at height 5,189,394, 6.3 times the number of blocks that one block in ten minutes since 2011-02-02 would have given and more than 5 times the 971,537 blocks of mainnet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Erratum of detail: the book says that the minimum difficulty of testnet is half that of Bitcoin, but chainparams.cpp gives mainnet and testnet3 the same proof-of-work limit 00000000ffff..., so the minimum difficulty is 1 on both. The sentence agrees with the Bitcoin Wiki and not with the code. The second rule, that a block more than 20 minutes after its parent may use the minimum difficulty, is right (pow.cpp uses 2 x 10 minutes) and holds for testnet3, testnet4 and regtest (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Incomplete list: the book's tip says that test networks use addresses beginning with m, n or tb1, but the test chains also use the prefix 2 for script-hash addresses (base58 version 196) and regtest uses bcrt1 (bech32 prefix bcrt), as its own listing shows; the nodes of the run produced m, 2, tb1q and tb1p on testnet4 and signet, and bcrt1q and bcrt1p on regtest (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Changed value: the book's listing of the default signet shows 143,619 blocks and a size of 769,525,915 bytes and says that the default signet has about 150,000 blocks and is about a gigabyte; on 2026-10-15 its tip was at height 326,440, 2.27 times as many, and Bitcoin Core assumes 24 GB of disk space for it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Contemporary developments

The default signet is operated by two contributors, as the book says, and the reason is visible in its challenge: a 71-byte script that is a 1-of-2 multisig of two 33-byte keys, so that either operator can sign a block. BIP 325 was assigned on 2019-03-20 to Karl-Johan Alm and Anthony Towns, and Bitcoin Core 0.21.0 added the support with one public signet maintained (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Alm and Towns, 2019); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2021); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Contemporary developments

The message-start bytes of a signet are not constants but the first four bytes of the double SHA-256 of the challenge script, so every custom signet has its own network magic: 0a03cf40 for the default signet, 54d26fbd for the challenge 51 and 7ec653a5 for the example of BIP 325, which lists the same value. The book does not mention this (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Alm and Towns, 2019); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

lecture.title: Chapter 11: The Blockchain
lecture.say: This deck explains the blockchain: the block and its 80-byte header, how a block is named and numbered, how blocks hold one another, how a merkle tree vouches for the transactions, and the test chains that practise all of it. Every example runs under Python 3.14.6 on the chapter's own library, and Bitcoin Core 31.1 was run on a test network, so its answers are Recorded and only read back here. The research package for chapter 11 holds the sources and the claims.
lecture.takeaway: What a block holds, how blocks are named and linked, how a merkle tree vouches for them, and the test chains. Bitcoin Core 31.1 results are Recorded.

lecture.say: This part opens a block and looks at every field of its header. It then asks how a block is named, how it is numbered, and what links it to its parent, and it ends with the case of two children of one parent. The first block, with its newspaper headline, is the story of the part.

lecture.title: A block is a header and its transactions
lecture.say: A block is an 80-byte header, a count of transactions, and the transactions. The first block of the test chain measured 285 bytes: 80 for the header, 1 for the count and 204 for its one transaction. The size field shown in the book's table is not part of the block but a prefix that Bitcoin Core writes in front of each block in its block files, which since release 28.0 are scrambled with a random key.
lecture.takeaway: A block is a header, a count and transactions; the size field is file storage

lecture.title: The 80-byte header and its six fields
lecture.say: The header holds six fields in 80 bytes: version, previous block hash, merkle root, time, bits and nonce, with numbers stored least significant byte first and hashes shown reversed. A block may be 4,000,000 bytes, so it can be 50,000 times its header. The version is no longer a counter: BIP 9 sets the top three bits to 001 for blocks that signal, and the remaining bits are flags.
lecture.takeaway: Six fields fill 80 bytes, and the version is now a set of flags

lecture.title: Time, target and nonce
lecture.say: The timestamp of a block must be greater than the median of the previous 11 block times and at most two hours ahead of the node's clock. The target is stored compactly in bits: 1d00ffff means a target of 0xffff followed by zeros, which is difficulty 1. Block 277,315 had a difficulty of 1,180,923,195, so its proof of work needed far more than the 4,294,967,296 values of the 32-bit nonce, which is why miners also change an extra nonce.
lecture.takeaway: The median of 11 times is the floor; the nonce alone is too small

lecture.say: The identifier of a block is the double SHA-256 of its 80-byte header, shown byte-reversed. lecture.say: Height counts the blocks since the first, which has height 0, and it is not a unique name, because two blocks can share a height during a fork. Since BIP 34 the height is written at the start of the coinbase script. A reward can be spent only 100 blocks later, and the test node refused a spend at depth 99 with premature-spend-of-coinbase.
lecture.takeaway: Height is a count, not a name; a reward matures after 100 blocks

lecture.title: Back-links make the history hard to change
lecture.say: Each header carries the hash of its parent, so the chain is a list in which every link depends on everything before it. On the test chain, ten consecutive headers linked correctly, and changing the fourth changed its hash, broke the link in the fifth, and meant that seven blocks would have to be mined again. The work of the chain is the sum of the work of its blocks, so the chain with the most work wins.
lecture.takeaway: Changing one old block means mining it and all later blocks again

lecture.title: Forks: two children, one parent
lecture.say: Two miners can find a block at about the same time, and then one parent has two children at the same height. The test node held both and called the one with more work active and the other a valid fork, and a block on top of one child settled it. The chance that an attacker catches up falls quickly with the number of blocks: with 10 percent of the power it is 0.2045873 from one block behind and 0.0002428 from six.
lecture.takeaway: A fork is settled by more work, and an old block is soon safe

lecture.title: Merkle trees
lecture.say: This part is about the hash tree that sits between a block's transactions and its header. It shows how the root is built, how a short path proves that one transaction belongs, and where the tree is weak: a duplicated hash and a 64-byte transaction. The story is that of its inventor, Ralph Merkle.
lecture.takeaway: How one 32-byte root vouches for every transaction in a block, and where the tree is weak.

lecture.title: The merkle tree: many transactions, one root
lecture.say: The transaction ids of a block are hashed in pairs, level by level, until one hash is left, and that merkle root goes into the header. For four transactions the levels have 4, 2 and 1 hashes, and the test node's root matched our own. When a level has an odd count, its last hash is paired with itself, which is why a copy of the last transaction gives the same root.
lecture.takeaway: Pairs are hashed upward; an odd hash is paired with itself

lecture.title: A merkle proof is a short path of hashes
lecture.say: A light client can check that a transaction is in a block with only the hashes along its path to the root, one for each level. For transaction 10 of 16 that is 4 hashes, 128 bytes, and following them reproduced the root of the header. The path grows with the logarithm of the block, 448 bytes for 16,000 transactions, so with the header a proof is 528 bytes; the book's claim of almost 10,000 times smaller is really 7,576 times.
lecture.takeaway: A proof is a few hashes, and the book's ratio of 10,000 is 7,576

lecture.title: Two weaknesses of the merkle tree
lecture.say: Because an odd hash is paired with itself, a list with the last transactions repeated has the same root as the original, so two different blocks can share one header. Bitcoin Core refuses the mutated block with bad-txns-duplicate, and on the test chain it kept the original. The second weakness is that an inner node is the hash of 64 bytes, so a transaction of exactly 64 bytes could be mistaken for one, which BIP 54 forbids.
lecture.takeaway: The tree has two known weaknesses, and the node defends against both

lecture.title: One small hash that vouches for a list
lecture.say: Ralph Merkle patented the hash tree in 1979, and the United States patent 4309569 was published on 5 January 1982 with Stanford University as assignee. In 1980 he wrote about tree authentication, and Satoshi Nakamoto's paper hashes the transactions of a block in such a tree and keeps only the root in the header. The 40 transactions of block 277,315 hashed in pairs up six levels to the root in its header.
lecture.takeaway: The story of 5 January 1982: who, where, when and what to read next

lecture.title: Test blockchains
lecture.say: This part is about the chains on which developers practise. They run the same code as the main chain but with different rules, prefixes and ports, and each solved a problem of the one before it. The stories are the flooding of testnet3 and the signature that a signet block must carry.
lecture.takeaway: Practice chains where coins cost nothing: testnet, signet and regtest, and their rules.

lecture.title: Several chains, one code base
lecture.say: The same program runs five chains, chosen by an option, each with its own data directory, port and address prefixes. The book's tip says that test addresses begin with m, n or tb1, but the test chains also use the prefix 2 for script addresses, and regtest uses bcrt1. Regtest halves its reward every 150 blocks, so 500 blocks earned 12,462.5 coins, as the book shows. No connection to a real network was made.
lecture.takeaway: One program runs five chains; the prefixes are more than the book lists

lecture.title: Testnet: flooded, then replaced
lecture.say: Testnet coins are worth nothing, so nothing stops a miner from flooding the chain. Testnet3 lets a block use minimum difficulty after twenty idle minutes, and its height is 6.3 times what one block in ten minutes would give; the book's size of 30 GB is far out of date too. Testnet4, specified in BIP 94, has its own genesis block and rules against the flooding. The heights are public figures; no test network was synchronised here.
lecture.takeaway: Testnet3 was flooded; testnet4 has rules against it

lecture.title: When the sandbox was flooded
lecture.say: On 4 May 2024 Jameson Lopp published how the minimum-difficulty rule of testnet3 lets miners create hundreds of blocks in a day. Testnet4 had its genesis block on 3 May 2024, and BIP 94, written by Fabian Jahr, bounds the time of the first block of a period; Bitcoin Core 28.0 added the network. BIP 94 notes that three years of blocks were mined on testnet3 in a few weeks, and testnet3 is now 33 times as long as testnet4.
lecture.takeaway: The story of 4 May 2024: who, where, when and what to read next

lecture.title: Signet: blocks need a signature
lecture.say: On a signet a block is valid only if it carries a signature that satisfies a challenge script, so the operators decide who may make blocks and the chain stays calm. The default signet's challenge is a one-of-two multisig, which is why the book says two contributors run it; a signet with the challenge 51 can be signed by anyone and ran on the test node. The network magic is derived from the challenge, so every signet has its own.
lecture.takeaway: A signet block needs a signature, so the chain stays calm

lecture.title: A test network with a doorman
lecture.say: BIP 325, Signet, was assigned on 20 March 2019 to Karl-Johan Alm and Anthony Towns: a block is valid only if it carries a solution to a challenge script, so the creators of a signet decide who may make blocks. Bitcoin Core 0.21.0 added the support, and personal signets are possible with the option -signetchallenge. The network magic is the start of the hash of the challenge, so every signet has its own, and the public one is 2.27 times as long as the book's listing.
